title: C++ STL Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Night-before revision of the C++ STL: sequence and associative containers, priority_queue, iterator invalidation, core <algorithm> calls, lambdas, and a complexity cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Sequence Containers: vector, deque, list
points: vector is a contiguous dynamic array: O(1) random access, amortized O(1) push_back, O(n) insert/erase in the middle; capacity grows geometrically (about 1.5x to 2x)
reserve(n) preallocates capacity without changing size(); resize(n) changes size and value-initializes new elements
deque is chunked blocks: O(1) push_front and push_back, O(1) random access, but not contiguous in memory
list is a doubly linked list: O(1) insert/erase at a known iterator, no random access, splice moves nodes in O(1), and it has no operator[]
Example: vector<int> v{3,1,2}; v.push_back(4); v.emplace_back(5); v.back(); v.pop_back(); v.erase(v.begin()+1); v.size()
Mistake: v[i] is unchecked while v.at(i) throws out_of_range; vector<bool> is a packed bitset, not a real container of bool

chapters.title: Associative Containers: map, unordered_map, set
points: map and set are ordered red-black trees: O(log n) find/insert/erase, iteration in sorted key order, keys unique (multimap and multiset allow duplicates)
unordered_map and unordered_set are hash tables: O(1) average, O(n) worst case, no ordering; a custom key type needs a hash function and operator==
map::operator[] inserts a default-constructed value when the key is missing; use find(k) != end() or count(k) to test without inserting, and at(k) to throw
Insert variants: insert(pair) does nothing if the key exists, emplace constructs in place, insert_or_assign overwrites, try_emplace avoids building the value if the key exists
Example: map<string,int> m; m["a"]++; for (auto& [k,v] : m) cout << k << v; auto it = m.lower_bound("b"); — lower_bound gives the first key >= x, upper_bound the first key > x
Mistake: reading m[k] in a const or lookup-only context silently grows the map; also a custom comparator must be a strict weak ordering (use < not <=)

chapters.title: priority_queue and Container Adaptors
points: priority_queue is a binary heap adaptor over vector: top() is O(1), push and pop are O(log n), and it is a max-heap by default
Min-heap: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq; the three template arguments are type, container, comparator

Custom order with a lambda: auto cmp = [](const P& a, const P& b){ return a.d > b.d; }; priority_queue, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp); — the comparator's logic is inverted, because 'less' means lower priority
stack and queue are adaptors over deque: only push, pop and top (or front/back) are exposed, with no iterators and no traversal

Mistake: calling top() or pop() on an empty container is undefined behavior, so check empty() first; pop() returns void, so read top() before pop(); you cannot update an element in place, so push a new one and skip stale entries

chapters.title: Iterators and Invalidation
points: An iterator is a pointer-like handle: begin() points at the first element, end() points one past the last and must never be dereferenced; categories run input, forward, bidirectional, random-access
vector: push_back may reallocate and invalidate all iterators, references and pointers; insert/erase invalidate everything from the change point onward
deque: insert/erase in the middle invalidates all iterators; push_front and push_back invalidate iterators but not references to elements
list, map and set: insert never invalidates; erase invalidates only the erased element's iterator; unordered containers: a rehash on insert invalidates iterators
Safe erase in a loop: for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end();) { if (pred(*it)) it = v.erase(it); else ++it; } — erase returns the next valid iterator
Mistake: erasing inside a range-for, or erasing with it++ on a vector; for a vector use the erase-remove idiom: v.erase(remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end())

chapters.title: <algorithm> Essentials and Lambdas
points: sort(first, last[, cmp]) is O(n log n) and needs random-access iterators, so it does not work on list (use list::sort); stable_sort preserves the order of equal elements; sort is not stable
Binary search on a sorted range, O(log n): binary_search returns a bool, lower_bound the first element >= x, upper_bound the first element > x; calling them on an unsorted range is undefined

Common calls: find, find_if, count_if, accumulate (in <numeric>, with a typed init such as 0LL), reverse, unique (needs sorted input and is paired with erase), max_element, min_element, next_permutation, iota

Lambda syntax: [capture](params){ body }; [=] captures by copy, [&] by reference, [x, &y] is mixed; use it as a comparator, sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b){ return a > b; }), or a predicate, count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [k](int x){ return x > k; })

Mistake: a comparator using <= breaks strict weak ordering and can crash sort; accumulate with init 0 on a vector<long long> overflows because the sum is accumulated as int; a [&] lambda that outlives its scope holds dangling references

chapters.title: Complexity Cheat Sheet
points: vector: access O(1), push_back amortized O(1), insert/erase middle O(n), find O(n); deque: access O(1), push/pop at both ends O(1), middle O(n)
list: insert/erase at iterator O(1), access and find O(n); map/set: find, insert, erase all O(log n), ordered; unordered_map/set: O(1) average, O(n) worst
priority_queue: top O(1), push/pop O(log n); building a heap from n elements via the range constructor is O(n); sort O(n log n); binary_search, lower_bound and upper_bound O(log n) on sorted ranges

Default pick: vector for almost everything, unordered_map for fast lookup, map when sorted order or range queries are needed, priority_queue for repeated min/max, deque for queues with front and back access
Checklist: reserve when the size is known, erase-remove for deletion, reference with auto& in loops, check empty() before top(), and use strict < in comparators
